edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 1, Paris 1844), Ad Scapulam, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Nos quidem neque expavescimus, neque pertimescimus ea, quae ab ignorantibus patimur: cum ad hanc sectam, utique suscepta conditione ejus, pacti venerimus, ut etiam animas nostras auctorati in has pugnas accedamus, ea quae Deus repromittit consequi optantes, et ea quae diversae vitae comminatur pati timentes. Denique cum omni saevitia vestra concertamus, etiam ultro erumpentes, magisque damnati quam absoluti gaudemus. Itaque hunc libellum non nobis timentes misimus, sed vobis et omnibus inimicis nostris, nedum amicis: ita enim disciplina jubemur diligere inimicos quoque, et orare pro eis qui nos persequuntur: ut haec sit perfecta et propria bonitas nostra, non communis. Amicos enim diligere omnium est, inimicos autem solorum christianorum. Qui ergo dolemus de ignorantia vestra, et miseremur erroris humani, et futura prospicimus, et signa eorum quotidie intentari videmus, necesse est vel hoc modo erumpere ad proponenda vobis ea, quae palam non vultis audire.
pass_a_gloss: We indeed neither are frightened nor do we fear those things which we suffer from ignorant people, since we have come to this sect, having undertaken its condition, so that we also engage our souls in these battles, wishing to attain those things which God promises and fearing to suffer those things which a different life threatens. Finally, since we contend with all your savagery, even bursting forth voluntarily, we rejoice more when condemned than when acquitted. And so we have sent this little book, not because we fear for ourselves, but for you and all our enemies, and not just for our friends; for our discipline commands us to love even enemies and to pray for those who persecute us, so that this may be our perfect and unique goodness, not common. For it is common to all to love friends, but it is unique to Christians alone to love enemies. Therefore, since we grieve over your ignorance and have pity on human error, and since we look to the future and see the signs of these things being prepared every day, it is necessary for us to burst forth in this way to propose to you those things which you do not want to hear openly.

rejected: we are commanded by our discipline

pass_b_english: We are not frightened, nor do we fear what we suffer at the hands of ignorant people. We entered this movement with eyes open, accepting its terms, so that we might commit our very lives to these battles—hoping to gain what God promises and dreading what a different life threatens. Indeed, we meet your every cruelty head-on, even stepping forward of our own accord, and we rejoice more when we are condemned than when we are acquitted. That is why we sent this pamphlet: not because we fear for ourselves, but for your sake and for the sake of all our enemies, not merely our friends. Our discipline commands us to love enemies, too, and to pray for those who persecute us, so that our goodness may be perfect and distinctive, not commonplace. After all, anyone can love friends; only Christians love enemies. Since we grieve over your ignorance, pity human error, watch the future, and see the signs of these things being prepared daily, we are compelled to speak out in this way and lay before you the truths you refuse to hear openly.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text. Pass A and Pass B maintain the nuances of the source, including the distinction between common goodness and Christian goodness, and the causal relationship regarding the author's motivation to write. All clauses are accounted for.
